extraction_notes.note: The paper cites with \lemref, \propref and \equref, which the finishing step does not treat as \ref commands; those dependencies were added by hand with basis 'named'.
Displays written with the undefined macros \be/\bea are not reported as numbered equations; the labelled ones (cited via \equref) were emitted as equation nodes with confidence 0.9.

The Gowers-Hatami theorem is stated twice (irrep version and regular-representation version) with different target spaces and separate proofs; kept as two nodes rather than merging under the repeated-statement rule.
Lemma 'Soundness of the BLR test' restates Theorem 1 in rejection form with an alternative Gowers-Hatami proof valid only conditionally; kept as its own node, linked by a mention edge.
Definition environments that specify a verifier step by step were retyped as algorithm (definition of a procedure).

Remark 'Pontryagin dual over direct product' states a standard theorem and was retyped theorem (external); Remark 'Group isomorphism' asserts and checks a result but was kept a remark as the author frames it as motivation.
The proofs of the two F_2 BLR theorems are empty environments in the source; no proof nodes were created for them.
The proof environment of Maschke's theorem only reports formalization status; kept as a proof node with no argument.

nodes.name: Field size q = p^s
nodes.statement: Throughout this section, let $q=p^s$ for a prime $p$ and $s\in\bbN$ with $s\ge 1$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Primitive p-th root of unity
nodes.statement: Let $\omega_p = e^{2\pi i/p}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Field trace
nodes.statement: The field trace $\Tr: \bbF_q \to \bbF_p$ is \[ \Tr(z) \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^{s-1} z^{p^i}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:field-trace

nodes.name: Base additive character
nodes.statement: The base additive character $\psi:\bbF_q\to\bbC$ is \[ \psi(z) \coloneqq \omega_p^{\Tr(z)}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:base-character

nodes.name: Additive characters
nodes.statement: For $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$, define the additive character $\chi_\alpha: \bbF_q^n\to\bbC$ by \[ \chi_\alpha(x) \coloneqq \psi(\inner{\alpha}{x}) = \omega_p^{\Tr(\inner{\alpha}{x})}, \] where $\inner{\alpha}{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i x_i\in\bbF_q$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:additive-character

nodes.name: Expectation
nodes.statement: For a function $h:\bbF_q^n\to\bbC$, define its uniform expectation by \[ \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}[h(x)] \coloneqq \frac{1}{q^n}\sum_{x\in\bbF_q^n} h(x). \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:expectation

nodes.name: Inner product
nodes.statement: For functions $h_1,h_2:\bbF_q^n\to\bbC$, define \[ \inner{h_1}{h_2} \coloneqq \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[h_1(x)\overline{h_2(x)}\right]. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:function-inner-product

nodes.name: $L_2$ norm
nodes.statement: For a function $h:\bbF_q^n\to\bbC$, define its $L_2$ norm by \[ \|h\|_2 \coloneqq \left(\bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[\abs{h(x)}^2\right]\right)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\inner{h}{h}}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:function-l2-norm

nodes.name: Fourier coefficient
nodes.statement: For $h:\bbF_q^n\to\bbC$ and $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$, define \[ \widehat h(\alpha) \coloneqq \inner{h}{\chi_\alpha} = \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[h(x)\overline{\chi_\alpha(x)}\right]. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:fourier-coefficient

nodes.name: Characters are orthonormal
nodes.statement: For every $\alpha,\beta\in\bbF_q^n$, \[ \inner{\chi_\alpha}{\chi_\beta} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha=\beta,\\ 0 & \text{if } \alpha\ne\beta. \end{cases} \]

If $\alpha= eta$, then $\alpha- eta=0$, so $\chi_{\alpha- eta}(x)=1$ for every $x\in bF_q^n$. Hence \[  bE_{x\in bF_q^n}\left[\chi_\alpha(x)\overline{\chi_ eta(x)}ight] =  bE_{x\in bF_q^n}[1] = 1. \] Now suppose $\alpha

Thus, as $x_j$ ranges uniformly over $ bF_q$, the value $\inner{\gamma}{x}$ also ranges uniformly over $ bF_q$. nodes.statement_short: Case split on $\alpha=\beta$; for $\alpha\ne\beta$ reduce to one coordinate and show the trace character sums to zero since trace fibers are equal-sized.

nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Case alpha = beta
nodes.statement:
If $\alpha=\beta$, then $\alpha-\beta=0$, so $\chi_{\alpha-\beta}(x)=1$ for every
$x\in\bbF_q^n$. Hence
\[
    \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[\chi_\alpha(x)\overline{\chi_\beta(x)}\right]
    =
    \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}[1]
    =
    1.
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Case alpha != beta
nodes.statement:
Now suppose $\alpha\ne\beta$. Let $\gamma \coloneqq \alpha-\beta$. Then $\gamma\ne 0$, so there exists
an index $j$ such that $\gamma_j\ne 0$. Fix all coordinates of $x$ except $x_j$. For the fixed
remaining coordinates, the map
\[
    x_j\mapsto \inner{\gamma}{x}
\]
has the form
\[
    x_j\mapsto \gamma_j x_j + c
\]
for some constant $c\in\bbF_q$. Since $\gamma_j\ne 0$, multiplication by $\gamma_j$ is a
bijection on $\bbF_q$, and therefore the affine map $x_j\mapsto \gamma_jx_j+c$ is also a
bijection on $\bbF_q$. Thus, as $x_j$ ranges uniformly over $\bbF_q$, the value
$\inner{\gamma}{x}$ also ranges uniformly over $\bbF_q$. Averaging first over $x_j$ and then
over the remaining coordinates gives
\[
    \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[\chi_\gamma(x)\right]
    =
    \bbE_{t\in\bbF_q}\left[\omega_p^{\Tr(t)}\right].
\]

It remains to show that this last average is zero. The trace map
$\Tr:\bbF_q\to\bbF_p$ is a nonzero $\bbF_p$-linear map, so every fiber of $\Tr$ has the same
cardinality. Since $\abs{\bbF_q}=q$ and $\abs{\bbF_p}=p$, each fiber has cardinality $q/p$.
Therefore
\begin{align*}
    \bbE_{t\in\bbF_q}\left[\omega_p^{\Tr(t)}\right]
    &=
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{t\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(t)} \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{r\in\bbF_p}
        \sum_{\substack{t\in\bbF_q\\ \Tr(t)=r}}
        \omega_p^r \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{r\in\bbF_p}\frac{q}{p}\omega_p^r \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{p}\sum_{r\in\bbF_p}\omega_p^r \\
    &=0,
\end{align*}
because the sum of all $p$-th roots of unity is zero. Hence, if $\alpha\ne\beta$, then
\[
    \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[\chi_\alpha(x)\overline{\chi_\beta(x)}\right]
    =
    0.
\]

remaining coordinates, the map
\[
    x_j\mapsto \inner{\gamma}{x}

nodes.statement_short: Affine bijection in $x_j$ reduces the average to a sum over $\bbF_q$.

nodes.name: Trace character sums to zero
nodes.statement:
It remains to show that this last average is zero. The trace map
$\Tr:\bbF_q\to\bbF_p$ is a nonzero $\bbF_p$-linear map, so every fiber of $\Tr$ has the same
cardinality. Since $\abs{\bbF_q}=q$ and $\abs{\bbF_p}=p$, each fiber has cardinality $q/p$.
Therefore
\begin{align*}
    \bbE_{t\in\bbF_q}\left[\omega_p^{\Tr(t)}\right]
    &=
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{t\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(t)} \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{r\in\bbF_p}
        \sum_{\substack{t\in\bbF_q\\ \Tr(t)=r}}
        \omega_p^r \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{r\in\bbF_p}\frac{q}{p}\omega_p^r \\
    &=
    \frac{1}{p}\sum_{r\in\bbF_p}\omega_p^r \\
    &=0,
\end{align*}
because the sum of all $p$-th roots of unity is zero.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.statement_short: Equal trace fibers reduce the sum to a sum of all $p$-th roots of unity, which is 0.

Hence, if $\alpha\ne\beta$, then
\[
    \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[\chi_\alpha(x)\overline{\chi_\beta(x)}\right]
    =
    0.
\]

Combining the two cases proves the stated orthogonality relation. The equivalent formulation

nodes.name: Fourier inversion
nodes.statement: For every function $h:\bbF_q^n\to\bbC$ we have \[ h(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}\widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha(x) \quad\text{for every }x\in\bbF_q^n. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:fourier-inversion

nodes.name: Proof of Fourier inversion
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:character-orthonormal}, the additive characters \[ \{\chi_\alpha : \alpha \in \mathbb F_q^n\} \] are orthonormal with respect to the inner product \[ \langle h_1,h_2\rangle = \mathbb E_{x\in \mathbb F_q^n} \left[h_1(x)\overline{h_2(x)}\right]. \] Moreover, these characters span the vector space of all complex-valued functions on \(\mathbb F_q^n\). Indeed, there are exactly \(q^n\) characters, and the space of functions \(\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb C\) has dimension \(q^n\). Since the characters are nonzero and pairwise orthogonal, they are linearly independent. Hence they form an orthonormal basis. Therefore every function \(h:\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb C\) has a unique expansion in this basis: \[ h = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} c_\alpha \chi_\alpha \] for some coefficients \(c_\alpha\in\mathbb C\). Taking the inner product of both sides with \(\chi_\beta\), we obtain \[ \langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} c_\alpha \langle \chi_\alpha,\chi_\beta\rangle . \] By orthonormality, all terms in the sum vanish except the term \(\alpha=\beta\), and \(\langle \chi_\beta,\chi_\beta\rangle=1\). Hence \[ \langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle = c_\beta . \] By definition of the Fourier coefficient, \[ \widehat h(\beta)=\langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle . \] Thus \(c_\beta=\widehat h(\beta)\) for every \(\beta\in\mathbb F_q^n\). Therefore \[ h = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} \widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha . \] Evaluating this identity at \(x\in\mathbb F_q^n\) gives the Fourier inversion formula \[ h(x) = \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n} \widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha(x). \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.statement_short: Characters form an orthonormal basis (dimension count); expand $h$ and read off coefficients by inner products.

nodes.name: Orthonormality
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lem:character-orthonormal}, the additive characters
\[
    \{\chi_\alpha : \alpha \in \mathbb F_q^n\}
\]
are orthonormal with respect to the inner product
\[
    \langle h_1,h_2\rangle
    =
    \mathbb E_{x\in \mathbb F_q^n}
    \left[h_1(x)\overline{h_2(x)}\right].
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Characters form a basis
nodes.statement:
Moreover, these characters span the vector space of all complex-valued
functions on \(\mathbb F_q^n\). Indeed, there are exactly \(q^n\) characters,
and the space of functions \(\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb C\) has dimension \(q^n\).
Since the characters are nonzero and pairwise orthogonal, they are linearly
independent. Hence they form an orthonormal basis.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.statement_short: Dimension count shows the characters form an orthonormal basis.

nodes.name: Expand in basis
nodes.statement:
Therefore every function \(h:\mathbb F_q^n\to\mathbb C\) has a unique expansion
in this basis:
\[
    h
    =
    \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n}
        c_\alpha \chi_\alpha
\]
for some coefficients \(c_\alpha\in\mathbb C\).
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Extract coefficients
nodes.statement:
Taking the inner product of
both sides with \(\chi_\beta\), we obtain
\[
    \langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle
    =
    \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n}
        c_\alpha \langle \chi_\alpha,\chi_\beta\rangle .
\]
By orthonormality, all terms in the sum vanish except the term
\(\alpha=\beta\), and \(\langle \chi_\beta,\chi_\beta\rangle=1\). Hence
\[
    \langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle = c_\beta .
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Identify coefficients
nodes.statement:
By definition of the Fourier coefficient,
\[
    \widehat h(\beta)=\langle h,\chi_\beta\rangle .
\]
Thus \(c_\beta=\widehat h(\beta)\) for every
\(\beta\in\mathbb F_q^n\).
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Evaluate
nodes.statement:
Therefore
\[
    h
    =
    \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n}
        \widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha .
\]
Evaluating this identity at \(x\in\mathbb F_q^n\) gives the Fourier inversion
formula
\[
    h(x)
    =
    \sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb F_q^n}
        \widehat h(\alpha)\chi_\alpha(x).
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Plancherel identity
nodes.statement: For every pair of functions $f,g:\bbF_q^n\to\bbC$, \[ \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat f(\alpha)\overline{\widehat g(\alpha)} = \inner{f}{g}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:fourier-plancherel

nodes.name: Proof of Plancherel
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:fourier-inversion}, \[ f=\sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}\widehat f(\alpha)\chi_\alpha . \] Taking the inner product with \(g\) and using linearity in the first argument gives \[ \inner{f}{g} = \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat f(\alpha)\inner{\chi_\alpha}{g}. \] Since \[ \inner{\chi_\alpha}{g} = \overline{\inner{g}{\chi_\alpha}} = \overline{\widehat g(\alpha)}, \] we obtain \[ \inner{f}{g} = \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat f(\alpha)\overline{\widehat g(\alpha)}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.statement_short: Expand $f$ by Fourier inversion and take the inner product with $g$.

nodes.name: Fourier inversion
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lem:fourier-inversion},
\[
    f=\sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}\widehat f(\alpha)\chi_\alpha .
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Linearity
nodes.statement:
Taking the inner product with \(g\) and using linearity in the first argument gives
\[
    \inner{f}{g}
    =
    \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}
        \widehat f(\alpha)\inner{\chi_\alpha}{g}.
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Conjugate symmetry
nodes.statement:
Since
\[
    \inner{\chi_\alpha}{g}
    =
    \overline{\inner{g}{\chi_\alpha}}
    =
    \overline{\widehat g(\alpha)},
\]
we obtain
\[
    \inner{f}{g}
    =
    \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}
        \widehat f(\alpha)\overline{\widehat g(\alpha)}.
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Parseval identity
nodes.statement: For every function $h:\bbF_q^n\to\bbC$, \[ \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}\abs{\widehat h(\alpha)}^2 = \|h\|_2^2. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:parseval-identity

nodes.name: Proof of Parseval
nodes.statement: Apply \cref{lem:fourier-plancherel} with \(f=g=h\): \[ \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat h(\alpha)\overline{\widehat h(\alpha)} = \inner{h}{h}. \] The left-hand side is \[ \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}\abs{\widehat h(\alpha)}^2, \] and by the definitions of the inner product and the $L_2$ norm, the right-hand side is \[ \inner{h}{h} = \bbE_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[\abs{h(x)}^2\right] = \|h\|_2^2. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Nonzero field elements
nodes.statement: Write \[ \bbF_q^\times \coloneqq \{c\in\bbF_q : c\ne 0\}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:nonzero-field-elements

nodes.name: Fourier expansion of a finite-field-valued function
nodes.statement: Let $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$. For each $c\in\bbF_q^\times$, define the $c$-phase lift \[ \fexp{\ff}{c}(x) \coloneqq \omega_p^{\Tr(c f(x))}. \] The Fourier expansion of $f$ is the set $\{\varphi_c\}_{c\in \bbF_q^\times}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.statement_short: The phase lifts $\varphi_c(x)=\omega_p^{\Tr(cf(x))}$, $c\ne0$, form the Fourier expansion of $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$.
nodes.label: def:fourier-expansion-field-valued

nodes.name: Character-sum indicator
nodes.statement: For every $u,v\in\bbF_q$, \[ \ind[u=v] = \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(c(u-v))}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: lem:character-sum-indicator

nodes.name: Proof of character-sum indicator
nodes.statement:

We prove that, for every \(t\in  bF_q\), \[ \ind[t=0] =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in bF_q}\psi(ct). \] The desired statement follows by taking \(t=u-v\). If \(t=0\), then \(ct=0\) for every \(c\in bF_q\), so \[  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in bF_q}\psi(ct) =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in bF_q}1 = 1. \] Now suppose \(t
eq 0\). Then multiplication by \(t\) is a bijection \( bF_q	o bF_q\), so \[ \sum_{c\in bF_q}\psi(ct) = \sum_{z\in bF_q}\psi(z). \] We claim that the latter sum is \(0\). Let \[ S \coloneqq \sum_{z\in bF_q}\psi(z). \] Since \(\Tr: bF_q	o bF_p\) is a nonzero \( bF_p\)-linear map, it is surjective. Hence there exists \(a\in bF_q\) such that \(\Tr(a)=1\). Using the bijection \(z\mapsto z+a\), we get \[ S = \sum_{z\in bF_q}\psi(z+a) = \sum_{z\in bF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z+a)} = \sum_{z\in bF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z)}\omega_p^{\Tr(a)} = \omega_p S. \] Since \(\omega_p
eq 1\), this implies \(S=0\). Therefore, when \(t
eq 0\), \[  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in bF_q}\psi(ct)=0. \] Combining the two cases gives \[ \ind[t=0] =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in bF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(ct)}. \] Substituting \(t=u-v\), we obtain \[ \ind[u=v] =  rac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in bF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(c(u-v))}. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $t=u-v$; case $t=0$ trivial, case $t\ne0$ the full character sum vanishes by a shift invariance argument.

nodes.name: Reduce to t
nodes.statement:
For each $z \in \bbF_q$ we define
\[
    \psi(z) \coloneqq \omega_p^{\Tr(z)}
\]
be the standard additive character of \(\bbF_q\). We prove that, for every
\(t\in \bbF_q\),
\[
    \ind[t=0]
    =
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\psi(ct).
\]
The desired statement follows by taking \(t=u-v\).
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi$ and reduce to the indicator of $t=0$.

nodes.name: Case t = 0
nodes.statement:
If \(t=0\), then \(ct=0\) for every \(c\in\bbF_q\), so
\[
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\psi(ct)
    =
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}1
    =
    1.
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Case t != 0
nodes.statement:
Now suppose \(t\neq 0\). Then multiplication by \(t\) is a bijection
\(\bbF_q\to\bbF_q\), so
\[
    \sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\psi(ct)
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z).
\]
We claim that the latter sum is \(0\). Let
\[
    S \coloneqq \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z).
\]
Since \(\Tr:\bbF_q\to\bbF_p\) is a nonzero \(\bbF_p\)-linear map, it is
surjective. Hence there exists \(a\in\bbF_q\) such that \(\Tr(a)=1\).
Using the bijection \(z\mapsto z+a\), we get
\[
    S
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z+a)
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z+a)}
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z)}\omega_p^{\Tr(a)}
    =
    \omega_p S.
\]
Since \(\omega_p\neq 1\), this implies \(S=0\). Therefore, when
\(t\neq 0\),
\[
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\psi(ct)=0.
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Change variables
nodes.statement:
Now suppose \(t\neq 0\). Then multiplication by \(t\) is a bijection
\(\bbF_q\to\bbF_q\), so
\[
    \sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\psi(ct)
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z).
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Claim: S = 0
nodes.statement:
We claim that the latter sum is \(0\). Let
\[
    S \coloneqq \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z).
\]
Since \(\Tr:\bbF_q\to\bbF_p\) is a nonzero \(\bbF_p\)-linear map, it is
surjective. Hence there exists \(a\in\bbF_q\) such that \(\Tr(a)=1\).
Using the bijection \(z\mapsto z+a\), we get
\[
    S
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z+a)
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z+a)}
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z)}\omega_p^{\Tr(a)}
    =
    \omega_p S.
\]
Since \(\omega_p\neq 1\), this implies \(S=0\).
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Pick a with Tr(a)=1
nodes.statement:
Let
\[
    S \coloneqq \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z).
\]
Since \(\Tr:\bbF_q\to\bbF_p\) is a nonzero \(\bbF_p\)-linear map, it is
surjective. Hence there exists \(a\in\bbF_q\) such that \(\Tr(a)=1\).
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Shift invariance
nodes.statement:
Using the bijection \(z\mapsto z+a\), we get
\[
    S
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\psi(z+a)
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z+a)}
    =
    \sum_{z\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(z)}\omega_p^{\Tr(a)}
    =
    \omega_p S.
\]
Since \(\omega_p\neq 1\), this implies \(S=0\).
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Conclude case
nodes.statement:
Therefore, when
\(t\neq 0\),
\[
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\psi(ct)=0.
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Combine and substitute
nodes.statement:
Combining the two cases gives
\[
    \ind[t=0]
    =
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(ct)}.
\]
Substituting \(t=u-v\), we obtain
\[
    \ind[u=v]
    =
    \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}\omega_p^{\Tr(c(u-v))}.
\]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields

nodes.name: Relative Hamming distance
nodes.statement: For $f,g:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$, define \[ \delta(f,g) \coloneqq \Pr_{x\in\bbF_q^n}\left[f(x)\ne g(x)\right]. \]
nodes.section: 1.1 Basic tools for the analysis of functions over finite fields
nodes.label: def:relative-hamming-distance

nodes.name: Linear functions
nodes.statement: For $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$, define the linear scalar function $\ell_\alpha:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$ by \[ \ell_\alpha(x) \coloneqq \inner{\alpha}{x}. \] A function $h:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$ is linear if $h=\ell_\alpha$ for some $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$. The finite set of all linear scalar functions is \[ \lin \coloneqq \left\{\ell_\alpha \mid \alpha\in\bbF_q^n\right\}. \]
nodes.label: def:linear-functions

nodes.name: Distance to linearity
nodes.statement: The distance from $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$ to linearity is \[ \delta(f,\lin) \coloneqq \min_{g\in\lin}\delta(f,g). \]
nodes.label: def:distance-to-linearity

nodes.name: Well-separatedness of linear functions
nodes.statement: For any distinct $f,g \in \lin$, one has $\delta(f,g)= 1-1/|\bbF|$.
nodes.label: lem:linear-set-well-separated

nodes.name: Proof of well-separatedness
nodes.statement: Let $a,b \in \bbF^n$ be the unique vectors such that $f(x) = \langle a, x\rangle$ and $g(x) = \langle b, x\rangle$ for each $x$. Let $c = a-b$, which must be a non-zero vector. In particular, there exists $i \in [n]$ such that $c_i \neq 0$. Take any permutation $\sigma: [n] \rightarrow [n]$ such that $\sigma(i)=n$. Then \begin{align*} \delta(f,g) & = 1- \Pr_{x \sim \bbF^n}[\langle c, x\rangle =0] \\ & = 1 - \frac{1}{|\bbF|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in \bbF}\frac{1}{|\bbF|}\sum_{x_n \in \bbF} \ind[c_i \cdot x_n = -\sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}] \\ & = 1 - \frac{1}{|\bbF|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in \bbF}\frac{1}{|\bbF|}\sum_{x_n \in \bbF} \ind[x_n = -c_i^{-1} \cdot \sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}] \end{align*} where the last equality follows because $c_i \neq 0$. Now note that $\ind[x_n = -c_i^{-1} \cdot \sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}]$ evaluates to $1$ for exactly one value of $x_n$. Thus we continue from above and get \begin{align*} \delta(f,g) = 1-\frac{1}{|\bbF|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in \bbF}\frac{1}{|\bbF|} = 1-\frac{1}{|\bbF|} \, . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The difference is a nonzero linear form; fixing all but one coordinate, exactly one value makes it vanish.

nodes.name: Difference vector
nodes.statement:
Let $a,b \in \bbF^n$ be the unique vectors such that $f(x) = \langle a, x\rangle$ and $g(x) = \langle b, x\rangle$ for each $x$.
Let $c = a-b$, which must be a non-zero vector. In particular, there exists $i \in [n]$ such that $c_i \neq 0$. Take any permutation $\sigma: [n] \rightarrow [n]$ such that $\sigma(i)=n$.

nodes.name: Rewrite distance
nodes.statement:
Then
\begin{align*}
    \delta(f,g) & = 1- \Pr_{x \sim \bbF^n}[\langle c, x\rangle =0] \\
    & = 1 - \frac{1}{|\bbF|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in \bbF}\frac{1}{|\bbF|}\sum_{x_n \in \bbF} \ind[c_i \cdot x_n = -\sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}] \\
    & = 1 - \frac{1}{|\bbF|^{n-1}}\sum_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1} \in \bbF}\frac{1}{|\bbF|}\sum_{x_n \in \bbF} \ind[x_n = -c_i^{-1} \cdot \sum_{j \in [n]\setminus {i}} c_j \cdot x_{\sigma(j)}] 
\end{align*}
where the last equality follows because $c_i \neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $\delta(f,g)$ via an indicator solved for $x_n$.

nodes.name: Count solutions
nodes.statement_short: Exactly one $x_n$ satisfies the indicator, giving $1-1/|\bbF|$.

nodes.name: Distance formula
nodes.statement: Let $f,g:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$. Let $\{\fexp{\ff}{c}\}_{c\in\bbF_q^\times}$ and $\{\fexp{\fg}{c}\}_{c\in\bbF_q^\times}$ be their Fourier expansions. Then \[ \delta(f,g) = 1-\frac{1}{q}\left(1+ \sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \inner{\fexp{\ff}{c}}{\fexp{\fg}{c}} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Relative Hamming distance expressed through inner products of the phase lifts.
nodes.label: lem:distance-formula

nodes.name: Proof of distance formula
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:character-sum-indicator}, \[ \Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)] = \bbE_x\left[\frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q} \omega_p^{\Tr(c(f(x)-g(x)))}\right]. \] The term $c=0$ contributes $1/q$. For $c\ne 0$, \[ \omega_p^{\Tr(c(f(x)-g(x)))} = \fexp{\ff}{c}(x)\overline{\fexp{\fg}{c}(x)}. \] Therefore \[ \Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)] =\frac{1}{q}\left(1+\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \inner{\fexp{\ff}{c}}{\fexp{\fg}{c}} \right), \] which gives the first formula after using $\delta(f,g)=1-\Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Write agreement probability with the character-sum indicator and separate the $c=0$ term.

nodes.name: Indicator expansion
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lem:character-sum-indicator},
\[
    \Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)]
    = \bbE_x\left[\frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}
        \omega_p^{\Tr(c(f(x)-g(x)))}\right].
\]

nodes.name: Split c = 0
nodes.statement:
The term $c=0$ contributes $1/q$. For $c\ne 0$,
\[
    \omega_p^{\Tr(c(f(x)-g(x)))}
    = \fexp{\ff}{c}(x)\overline{\fexp{\fg}{c}(x)}.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Separate $c=0$; other terms are products of phase lifts.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Therefore
\[
    \Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)]
    =\frac{1}{q}\left(1+\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times}
        \inner{\fexp{\ff}{c}}{\fexp{\fg}{c}}
    \right),
\]
which gives the first formula after using
$\delta(f,g)=1-\Pr_x[f(x)=g(x)]$.

nodes.name: Fourier expansion of a linear function
nodes.statement: Fix $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$ and let $\{\lambda_c\}_{c \in \bbF_q^\times}$ be the Fourier expansion of $\ell_\alpha$. Then \[ \fexp{\lambda}{c}=\chi_{c\alpha}. \]
assumptions: let $\{\lambda_c\}_{c \in \bbF_q^\times}$ be the Fourier expansion of $\ell_\alpha$
nodes.label: lem:linear-function-fourier-expansion

nodes.name: Proof of linear Fourier expansion
nodes.statement: For every $x\in\bbF_q^n$, \[ \fexp{\lambda}{c}(x) = \omega_p^{\Tr(c\inner{\alpha}{x})} = \omega_p^{\Tr(\inner{c\alpha}{x})} = \chi_{c\alpha}(x). \]

nodes.name: Linear Fourier score
nodes.statement: For $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$ and $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$, define the linear Fourier score of $f$ at $\alpha$ by \[ S_\alpha(f) \coloneqq \sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{c}}(c\alpha), \] where $\{\fexp{\ff}{c}\}_{c \in \bbF_q^\times}$ is the Fourier expansion of $f$.
nodes.label: def:linear-fourier-score

nodes.name: Distance to linearity in Fourier form
nodes.statement: Let $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$ have Fourier expansion $\{\fexp{\ff}{c}\}_{c\in\bbF_q^\times}$. Then \[ \delta(f,\lin) = 1-\frac{1}{q}\left(1+ \max_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} S_\alpha(f) \right). \] Moreover, for every $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$, the score $S_\alpha(f)$ is real and satisfies $-1\le S_\alpha(f)\le q-1$.
conclusions:
the score $S_\alpha(f)$ is real and
satisfies $-1\le S_\alpha(f)\le q-1$
nodes.statement_short: Distance to linearity equals $1-(1+\max_\alpha S_\alpha(f))/q$, with each score real in $[-1,q-1]$.
nodes.label: lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier

nodes.name: Proof of Fourier form of distance
nodes.statement: Apply \cref{lem:distance-formula} with $g=\ell_\alpha$ and use \cref{lem:linear-function-fourier-expansion}. This gives \[ \delta(f,\ell_\alpha) =1-\frac{1}{q}\left(1+ S_\alpha(f) \right). \] Taking the minimum over $\alpha$ gives the claimed formula for $\delta(f,\lin)$. For fixed $\alpha$, the same formula expresses $S_\alpha(f)$ as $q(1-\delta(f,\ell_\alpha))-1$. Hence $S_\alpha(f)$ is real, and since $0\le \delta(f,\ell_\alpha)\le 1$, we get $-1\le S_\alpha(f)\le q-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the distance formula with $g=\ell_\alpha$ and minimize over $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Distance to one linear function
nodes.statement:
Apply \cref{lem:distance-formula} with $g=\ell_\alpha$ and use
\cref{lem:linear-function-fourier-expansion}. This gives
\[
    \delta(f,\ell_\alpha)
    =1-\frac{1}{q}\left(1+
        S_\alpha(f)
    \right).
\]

nodes.name: Minimize
nodes.statement:
Taking the minimum over $\alpha$ gives the claimed formula for
$\delta(f,\lin)$.

nodes.name: Range of score
nodes.statement:
For fixed $\alpha$, the same formula expresses $S_\alpha(f)$ as
$q(1-\delta(f,\ell_\alpha))-1$. Hence $S_\alpha(f)$ is real, and since
$0\le \delta(f,\ell_\alpha)\le 1$, we get $-1\le S_\alpha(f)\le q-1$.

nodes.name: Finite-field BLR test
nodes.statement: Given oracle access to $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$, the finite-field BLR verifier $\BLRVerifier$ samples $a,b\in\bbF_q^\times$ and $x,y\in\bbF_q^n$ independently and uniformly at random, and accepts iff \[ a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by). \] That is, \[ \BLRVerifier=1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by). \]
nodes.statement_short: Sample nonzero scalars $a,b$ and points $x,y$; accept iff $af(x)+bf(y)=f(ax+by)$.
nodes.label: def:finite-field-blr-test

nodes.name: Sample
nodes.statement: samples $a,b\in\bbF_q^\times$ and $x,y\in\bbF_q^n$ independently and uniformly at random,

nodes.name: Accept test
nodes.statement:
accepts iff
\[
    a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by).
\]

nodes.name: Completeness of the finite-field BLR test
nodes.statement: If $f\in\lin$, then \[ \Pr[\BLRVerifier=1]=1. \]
nodes.label: lem:blr-completeness

nodes.name: Proof of BLR completeness
nodes.statement: If $f=\ell_\alpha$ for some $\alpha\in\bbF_q^n$, then for every $a,b\in\bbF_q^\times$ and $x,y\in\bbF_q^n$, \[ f(ax+by) =\inner{\alpha}{ax+by} =a\inner{\alpha}{x}+b\inner{\alpha}{y} =a f(x)+b f(y). \] Thus the verifier accepts for every choice of randomness.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity of $\ell_\alpha$ makes every test pass.

nodes.name: Exact BLR acceptance formula
nodes.statement: Let $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$. Then \[ \Pr[\BLRVerifier=1] = \frac{1}{q}\left(1+\frac{1}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} S_\alpha(f)^3 \right). \]
nodes.label: lem:exact-blr-acceptance

nodes.name: Proof of exact acceptance formula
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:character-sum-indicator}, for fixed $a,b,x,y$, \[ \ind[a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by)] =\frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q} \omega_p^{\Tr(c(a f(x)+b f(y)-f(ax+by)))}. \] Taking expectation gives \[ \Pr[\BLRVerifier=1] =\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{q}\bbE_{a,b,x,y} \left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \fexp{\ff}{ca}(x)\fexp{\ff}{cb}(y) \fexp{\ff}{-c}(ax+by) \right]. \] Expand the three complex-valued functions into their Fourier expansions: \begin{align*} &\bbE_{a,b,x,y} \left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \fexp{\ff}{ca}(x)\fexp{\ff}{cb}(y) \fexp{\ff}{-c}(ax+by) \right] \\ &=\bbE_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{ca}}(\alpha) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{cb}}(\beta) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{-c}}(\gamma) \bbE_{x,y}\left[ \chi_\alpha(x)\chi_\beta(y)\chi_\gamma(ax+by) \right] \right]. \end{align*} Since \[ \chi_\gamma(ax+by)=\chi_{a\gamma}(x)\chi_{b\gamma}(y), \] \cref{lem:character-orthonormal} implies that the inner expectation is $1$ exactly when \[ \alpha+a\gamma=0 \quad\text{and}\quad \beta+b\gamma=0, \] and is $0$ otherwise. Therefore the last display equals \[ \bbE_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{ca}}(\alpha) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{cb}}(a^{-1}b\alpha) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{-c}}(-a^{-1}\alpha) \right]. \] Substitute $\alpha=ca\eta$. Then this becomes \[ \bbE_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times} \sum_{\eta\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{ca}}(ca\eta) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{cb}}(cb\eta) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{-c}}(-c\eta) \right]. \] As $a,b,c$ range over $\bbF_q^\times$, so do $ca$, $cb$, and $-c$. Hence this equals \[ \frac{1}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\eta\in\bbF_q^n} \left(\sum_{d\in\bbF_q^\times} \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{d}}(d\eta) \right)^3 =\frac{1}{(q-1)^2}\sum_{\eta\in\bbF_q^n}S_\eta(f)^3. \] Substituting into the expression for $\Pr[\BLRVerifier=1]$ proves the claim.
nodes.statement_short: Write acceptance with the character-sum indicator, Fourier-expand the phase lifts, and collapse with character orthogonality. The key step is the substitution $\alpha=ca\eta$ that turns the triple sum into a cube of scores.

nodes.name: Indicator expansion
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lem:character-sum-indicator}, for fixed $a,b,x,y$,
\[
    \ind[a f(x)+b f(y)=f(ax+by)]
    =\frac{1}{q}\sum_{c\in\bbF_q}
        \omega_p^{\Tr(c(a f(x)+b f(y)-f(ax+by)))}.
\]
Taking expectation gives
\[
    \Pr[\BLRVerifier=1]
    =\frac{1}{q}+\frac{1}{q}\bbE_{a,b,x,y}
        \left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times}
        \fexp{\ff}{ca}(x)\fexp{\ff}{cb}(y)
        \fexp{\ff}{-c}(ax+by)
        \right].
\]

nodes.name: Fourier expand
nodes.statement_short: Expand phase lifts in Fourier series.

nodes.name: Orthogonality collapse
nodes.statement:
Since
\[
    \chi_\gamma(ax+by)=\chi_{a\gamma}(x)\chi_{b\gamma}(y),
\]
\cref{lem:character-orthonormal} implies that the inner expectation is $1$ exactly when
\[
    \alpha+a\gamma=0
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    \beta+b\gamma=0,
\]
and is $0$ otherwise. Therefore the last display equals
\[
    \bbE_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times}
    \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}
    \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{ca}}(\alpha)
    \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{cb}}(a^{-1}b\alpha)
    \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{-c}}(-a^{-1}\alpha)
    \right].
\]
nodes.statement_short: Character orthogonality forces $\beta,\gamma$ in terms of $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Substitute
nodes.statement:
Substitute $\alpha=ca\eta$. Then this becomes
\[
    \bbE_{a,b}\left[\sum_{c\in\bbF_q^\times}
    \sum_{\eta\in\bbF_q^n}
    \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{ca}}(ca\eta)
    \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{cb}}(cb\eta)
    \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{-c}}(-c\eta)
    \right].
\]

nodes.name: Reindex
nodes.statement_short: Reindex to a cube of scores.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Substituting into the expression for $\Pr[\BLRVerifier=1]$ proves the claim.

nodes.name: Second moment bound
nodes.statement: For every $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$, one has \[ \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} S_\alpha(f)^2 \le (q-1)^2. \]
nodes.label: lem:second-moment-bound

nodes.name: Proof of second moment bound
nodes.statement: Expanding the square gives \[ \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} S_\alpha(f)^2 =\sum_{a,b\in\bbF_q^\times} \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{a}}(a\alpha) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{b}}(b\alpha). \] For fixed $a,b\in\bbF_q^\times$, Cauchy-Schwarz and \cref{lem:parseval-identity} give \begin{align*} \abs{\sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{a}}(a\alpha) \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{b}}(b\alpha)} &\le \left(\sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}\abs{\widehat{\fexp{\ff}{a}}(a\alpha)}^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}\abs{\widehat{\fexp{\ff}{b}}(b\alpha)}^2\right)^{1/2} \\ &=1. \end{align*} The equality uses that multiplication by $a$ and by $b$ permutes $\bbF_q^n$, and that Parseval plus $\abs{\fexp{\ff}{a}(x)}=\abs{\fexp{\ff}{b}(x)}=1$ for every $x$ make both squared $L_2$ norms equal to \(1\). Summing over the $(q-1)^2$ choices of $(a,b)$ gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the square, bound each cross term by Cauchy-Schwarz and Parseval, sum over $(a,b)$.

nodes.name: Expand square
nodes.statement:
Expanding the square gives
\[
    \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n} S_\alpha(f)^2
    =\sum_{a,b\in\bbF_q^\times}
        \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}
        \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{a}}(a\alpha)
        \widehat{\fexp{\ff}{b}}(b\alpha).
\]
nodes.statement_short: Expand the square of the score.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Schwarz
nodes.statement_short: Each cross term is at most 1 by Cauchy-Schwarz and Parseval.

nodes.name: Sum
nodes.statement: Summing over the $(q-1)^2$ choices of $(a,b)$ gives the result.

nodes.name: Soundness of the finite-field BLR test
nodes.statement: For every function $f:\bbF_q^n\to\bbF_q$, one has \[ \Pr[\BLRVerifier=1] \le 1-\delta(f,\lin). \]
nodes.label: thm:finite-field-blr-soundness

nodes.name: Proof of finite-field BLR soundness
nodes.statement: Let $S_\alpha(f)$ be as in \cref{def:linear-fourier-score}, and let \[ M \coloneqq \max_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}S_\alpha(f). \] By \cref{lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier}, \[ 1-\delta(f,\lin)=\frac{1}{q}(1+M). \] By \cref{lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier}, each $S_\alpha(f)$ is real and $S_\alpha(f)\le M$. Therefore $S_\alpha(f)^3\le M S_\alpha(f)^2$ for every $\alpha$, because $S_\alpha(f)^2\ge 0$. Using \cref{lem:exact-blr-acceptance} and \cref{lem:second-moment-bound}, \begin{align*} \Pr[\BLRVerifier=1] &=\frac{1}{q}\left(1+\frac{1}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}S_\alpha(f)^3\right) \\ &\le \frac{1}{q}\left(1+\frac{M}{(q-1)^2} \sum_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}S_\alpha(f)^2\right) \\ &\le \frac{1}{q}(1+M) \\ &=1-\delta(f,\lin). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $S_\alpha^3\le M S_\alpha^2$ with $M=\max S_\alpha$, then combine the exact acceptance formula with the second moment bound.

nodes.name: Max score
nodes.statement:
Let $S_\alpha(f)$ be as in \cref{def:linear-fourier-score}, and let
\[
    M \coloneqq \max_{\alpha\in\bbF_q^n}S_\alpha(f).
\]

nodes.name: Distance via M
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier},
\[
    1-\delta(f,\lin)=\frac{1}{q}(1+M).
\]

nodes.name: Cubic bound
nodes.statement:
By \cref{lem:distance-to-linearity-fourier}, each $S_\alpha(f)$ is real and
$S_\alpha(f)\le M$.
Therefore $S_\alpha(f)^3\le M S_\alpha(f)^2$ for every $\alpha$, because
$S_\alpha(f)^2\ge 0$.

nodes.name: Chain bounds
nodes.statement_short: Combine exact formula and second-moment bound.

nodes.name: sigma inner product
nodes.statement: The $\sigma$ inner product between matrices $A$ and $B$ is defined as \be \inner{A}{B}_{\sigma} = \Tr(A^* B \sigma), \ee where $\sigma \geq 0$ and $A^*$ denotes conjugate-transpose.
nodes.label: sigmaInner

nodes.name: (epsilon, sigma)-representation
nodes.statement: Given a finite group \(G\), an integer \(d \geq 1, \varepsilon \geq 0\), and a \(d\)-dimensional positive semidefinite matrix \(\sigma\) with trace 1 , an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) is a map \(f: G \rightarrow U_{d}(\mathbb{C})\), to the \(d \times d\) unitary matrices, such that \be \mathbb{E}_{x, y \in G} \Re\left(\left\langle f(x)^{*} f(y), f\left(x^{-1} y\right)\right\rangle_{\sigma}\right) \geq 1-\varepsilon, \ee where $\Re$ denotes taking real part of the inner product.
nodes.statement_short: An approximate representation: a unitary-valued map on $G$ whose $\sigma$-correlation with $f(x^{-1}y)$ averages at least $1-\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: approx-representation

nodes.name: sigma-norm square
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma$ be positive semidefinite and let $A, B$ be matrices of the same dimension. Then \[ \|A - B\|_\sigma^2 = \|A\|_\sigma^2 + \|B\|_\sigma^2 - 2\,\Re\inner{A}{B}_\sigma. \]
assumptions: let $A, B$ be matrices of the same dimension
nodes.label: sigmaNormSqSub

nodes.name: Proof of sigma-norm square
nodes.statement: Expanding by linearity of the inner product, \[ \|A-B\|_\sigma^2 = \Re\inner{A-B}{A-B}_\sigma = \|A\|_\sigma^2 + \|B\|_\sigma^2 - \Re\inner{A}{B}_\sigma - \Re\inner{B}{A}_\sigma. \] Since $\sigma$ is Hermitian, $\inner{B}{A}_\sigma = \overline{\inner{A}{B}_\sigma}$, so the two cross terms have the same real part, yielding $-2\,\Re\inner{A}{B}_\sigma$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand by linearity and use Hermitian symmetry.

nodes.name: Group representation
nodes.statement:
In general, a representation of a group \(G\) on a vector space \(V\) over a
field \(k\) is a homomorphism from \(G\) to the linear endomorphisms of \(V\).
differentia: from \(G\) to the linear endomorphisms of \(V\)

nodes.name: Unitary representation
nodes.statement:
We call a representation \emph{unitary} when its image lies in the unitary
group; in the finite-dimensional matrix setting used below this means a
homomorphism \(\rho : G \to U(V)\).
differentia:
its image lies in the unitary
group

nodes.name: Regular representation
nodes.statement: Let $R: G \rightarrow \mathbb{C}[G]$ be a regular representation where $\{\ket{g}, g\in G\}$ forms a basis of \(\mathbb{C}[G]\). The representation is given by \be R(x) \ket{g} = \ket{xg}. \ee
nodes.label: RegularRep

nodes.name: Maschke's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and let $\rho : G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional representation over $\mathbb{C}$. Then $\rho$ is completely reducible. In particular, there exists a decomposition \be \rho \cong \bigoplus_{m} r_m \, \rho_m, \ee where $\{\rho_m\}$ is a set of inequivalent irreducible representations of $G$, and $r_m \in \mathbb{Z}^+$ are the multiplicities.
assumptions: let $\rho : G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional representation over $\mathbb{C}$
nodes.label: Maschke

nodes.name: Formalization note for Maschke's theorem
nodes.statement: Maschke's theorem is partially formalized in $\texttt{Mathlib.RepresentationTheory.Maschke}$ but incomplete. Filippo Berta, Jonathan Conrad, and Younous Malliefer are formalizing this.
nodes.statement_short: No argument: notes Maschke is partially in Mathlib and being formalized.

nodes.name: Decomposition of the regular representation
nodes.statement: Let $R : G \to \mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}[G])$ be the regular representation of a finite group $G$. Then \be R \cong \bigoplus_{\rho \in \widehat{G}} d_\rho \, \rho, \ee where $\widehat{G}$ is a complete set of inequivalent irreducible representations of $G$, and $d_\rho = \dim(V_\rho)$ is the dimension of $\rho$.
assumptions: $R : G \to \mathrm{GL}(\mathbb{C}[G])$ be the regular representation of a finite group $G$
nodes.label: RegDecompIrrep

nodes.name: Proof sketch of regular representation decomposition
nodes.statement: This can be proven using Maschke's theorem in \ref{Maschke} to decompose into irreps with multiplicity. Then use character orthogonality theorem in mathlib $\texttt{FDRep.char\_orthonormal}$ to show the multiplicity equals irrep dimension. A more formal statement is given by the Peter-Weyl theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose by Maschke, then use character orthonormality to show multiplicity equals dimension.

nodes.name: Apply Maschke
nodes.statement: This can be proven using Maschke's theorem in \ref{Maschke} to decompose into irreps with multiplicity.

nodes.name: Character orthogonality
nodes.statement: Then use character orthogonality theorem in mathlib $\texttt{FDRep.char\_orthonormal}$ to show the multiplicity equals irrep dimension.

nodes.name: Peter-Weyl pointer
nodes.statement: A more formal statement is given by the Peter-Weyl theorem.

nodes.name: Character of regular representation
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $\sum_\rho$ denotes summing over the complete set of inequivalent irreps $\hat{G}$ \be \sum_{\rho \in \hat{G}} d_{\rho} \operatorname{Tr}(\rho(x))=|G| \delta_{x, e}. \ee
nodes.label: regular_repr_character

nodes.name: Regular representation character identity
nodes.statement: \sum_{\rho \in \hat{G}} d_{\rho} \operatorname{Tr}(\rho(x))=|G| \delta_{x, e}.

nodes.name: Proof sketch of regular character identity
nodes.statement: The proof uses decomposition of regular representation and definition of character.
nodes.statement_short: From the regular representation decomposition and the definition of character.

nodes.name: Group Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Let $f: G \rightarrow U_d(\cc)$ be a map and \(\rho: G \rightarrow U_{d_{\rho}}(\mathbb{C})\) be a unitary irrep. The fourier transform of $f$ at the representation $\rho$ is denoted by $\hat{f}$: \be \hat{f}(\rho)=\mathbb{E}_{x \in G} f(x) \otimes \overline{\rho(x)}, \ee where $\overline{\rho(x)}$ denotes complex conjugate of $\rho(x)$.
nodes.definiendum: fourier transform of $f$ at the representation $\rho$
nodes.label: GroupFourier

nodes.name: Gowers-Hatami theorem
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\varepsilon \geq 0\), and \(f: G \rightarrow U_{d}(\mathbb{C})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\). Then there exists a \(d^{\prime} \geq d\), an isometry \(V: \mathbb{C}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{d^{\prime}}\), and a representation \(g: G \rightarrow U_{d^{\prime}}(\mathbb{C})\) such that \be \mathbb{E}_{x \in G}\left\|f(x)-V^{*} g(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \leq 2 \varepsilon. \ee
conclusions: there exists a \(d^{\prime} \geq d\), an isometry \(V: \mathbb{C}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{d^{\prime}}\), and a representation \(g: G \rightarrow U_{d^{\prime}}(\mathbb{C})\) such that
nodes.statement_short: Every $(\varepsilon,\sigma)$-approximate representation is $2\varepsilon$-close in $\sigma$-norm to a compressed exact representation.
nodes.label: gowers-hatami

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Gowers-Hatami via irreps
nodes.statement: The theorem is due to Gowers and Hatami~\cite{GowHat17}; the constructive proof below follows Vidick's lecture notes, Theorem 2.3~\cite{VidickQMATH22}. In particular, the proof is constructive. The isometry is defined as \(V: \mathbb{C}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{C}^{d} \otimes\left(\oplus_{\rho} \mathbb{C}^{d_{\rho}} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_{\rho}}\right)\) by \be V u = \bigoplus_{\rho} d_{\rho}^{1 / 2} \sum_{i=1}^{d_{\rho}}\left(\hat{f}(\rho)\left(u \otimes e_{i}\right)\right) \otimes e_{i}. \ee And the exact representation is defined as \be g(x)=\bigoplus_{\rho}\left(I_{d} \otimes I_{d_{\rho}} \otimes \rho(x)\right). \ee The proof requires the following two ingredients: \begin{enumerate} \item $V$ is an isometry: \be V^{*} V = \I_d \ee \item The isometry ``averages'' over group multiplication. For any \(x \in G\), \be V^{*} g(x) V = \mathbb{E}_{z} f(z)^{*} f(z x). \ee \end{enumerate} Both ingredients follow from the key identity over the regular representation in \equref{eq:regular-repr-characterr}.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the isometry from Fourier coefficients and the exact representation as a sum of irreps; isometry and averaging follow from the regular character identity.

The proof requires the following two ingredients:

        \item $V$ is an isometry:

        V^{*} V  = \I_d
        \ee 
        \item The isometry ``averages'' over group multiplication. For any \(x \in G\),

nodes.name: V is an isometry
nodes.statement:
$V$ is an isometry:
        \be
        V^{*} V  = \I_d
        \ee

The isometry ``averages'' over group multiplication. For any \(x \in G\),

nodes.name: Gowers-Hatami pair-correlation
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\varepsilon \geq 0\), and \(\rho: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) on space $\mathcal{H}$. Define the pair-correlation of $\rho$ as: \be \mathcal{C}(\rho) := \EE_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle \rho(y)\rho(x), \rho(yx) \rangle_\sigma. \ee Then there exists an isometry \(V: \mathcal{H} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) to a different space $\mathcal{H}^\prime$, and an exact representation \(\rho^\prime: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H}^\prime)\) such that the average correlation between $\rho$ and $\rho^\prime$ is exactly the pair-correlation, which is bounded by $1-\varepsilon$: \be \EE_{x \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\rangle_{\sigma} = \mathcal{C}(\rho) \geq 1-\varepsilon. \ee
assumptions: \(\rho: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) on space $\mathcal{H}$
conclusions:
there exists an isometry \(V: \mathcal{H} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) to a different space $\mathcal{H}^\prime$, 
and an exact representation \(\rho^\prime: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H}^\prime)\) such that the average correlation between $\rho$ and $\rho^\prime$ is exactly the pair-correlation, which is bounded by $1-\varepsilon$
nodes.statement_short: The regular-representation dilation of an approximate representation has average correlation equal to its pair-correlation, at least $1-\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: gowers-hatami-correlation

nodes.name: Proof of pair-correlation lemma
nodes.statement:
Here $\mathcal{H}^\prime = L(G, \mathcal{H})$ is the space of functions $f: G 	o \mathcal{H}$. Let the isometry be defined by the action of the approximate representation on a state $u\in \mathcal{H}$ as  ea &V:& \mathcal{H} 	o L(G, \mathcal{H}), \ & V(u):& G 	o \mathcal{H}, \quad x \mapsto ho(x)(u), \quad  orall x \in G. \eea The adjoint map $V^*$ is defined as the unique map such that for all $u \in \mathcal{H}$ and $f \in L(G, \mathcal{H})$,  e \langle V(u), f angle_{L(G, \mathcal{H})} = \langle u, V^*(f) angle_{\mathcal{H}}. \ee In particular, $V^*$ is explicitly given by the group average:  ea &V^*:& L(G, \mathcal{H}) 	o \mathcal{H}, \ &V^*(f)& = \EE_{x \in G} \left[ ho^*(x) f(x) ight]. \eea The exact representation is given by the right regular representation on $L(G, \mathcal{H})$:  ea &ho^\prime:& G 	o U(L(G, \mathcal{H})), \ &(ho^\prime(x)f)(y)& = f(yx), \quad  orall x,y \in G. \eea $V$ is an isometry because $ho(x)$ is unitary, yielding:  e V^* V(u) = \EE_{x \in G} \left[ ho^*(x) ho(x)(u) ight] = \EE_{x \in G} [u] = u. \ee The compression of the exact representation ``averages'' over group multiplication. For any $u \in \mathcal{H}$:  ea V^* ho^\prime(x) V(u) & = & \EE_{y \in G} \left[ ho^*(y) (ho^\prime(x)ho(y))(u) ight] 
onumber \ & = & \EE_{y \in G} \left[ ho^*(y) ho(yx)(u) ight]. \eea Substituting the average property from ~\equref{eq:isometry-average} into the inner product, and using the unitarity of $ho(y)$ to rewrite the adjoints ($\langle A, B^* C angle_\sigma = \langle B A, C angle_\sigma$), we obtain:  ea \EE_{x \in G} \Re \langle ho(x), V^* ho^\prime(x) Vangle_\sigma & = & \EE_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle ho(x), ho^*(y) ho(yx) angle_\sigma 
onumber \ & = & \EE_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle ho(y)ho(x), ho(yx) angle_\sigma 
onumber \ & = & \mathcal{C}(ho). \eea By the definition of an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate representation, the pair-correlation inherently satisfies $\mathcal{C}(ho) \geq 1 - \varepsilon$, which concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Construct $V(u)=(x\mapsto\rho(x)u)$ into $L(G,\mathcal H)$ with the right regular representation; compute $V^*\rho'(x)V$ as a group average and substitute into the correlation.

nodes.name: Define isometry
nodes.statement:
Here $\mathcal{H}^\prime = L(G, \mathcal{H})$ is the space of functions $f: G \to \mathcal{H}$.
    
    Let the isometry be defined by the action of the approximate representation on a state $u\in \mathcal{H}$ as
    \bea
    &V:& \mathcal{H} \to L(G, \mathcal{H}), \\
    & V(u):& G \to \mathcal{H}, \quad x \mapsto \rho(x)(u), \quad \forall x \in G.
    \eea

nodes.name: Adjoint
nodes.statement:
The adjoint map $V^*$ is defined as the unique map such that for all $u \in \mathcal{H}$ and $f \in L(G, \mathcal{H})$,
    \be
    \langle V(u), f \rangle_{L(G, \mathcal{H})} = \langle u, V^*(f) \rangle_{\mathcal{H}}.
    \ee

    In particular, $V^*$ is explicitly given by the group average:
    \bea
    &V^*:& L(G, \mathcal{H}) \to \mathcal{H}, \\
    &V^*(f)& = \EE_{x \in G} \left[ \rho^*(x) f(x) \right].
    \eea

nodes.name: Right regular representation
nodes.statement:
The exact representation is given by the right regular representation on $L(G, \mathcal{H})$:
    \bea
    &\rho^\prime:& G \to U(L(G, \mathcal{H})), \\
    &(\rho^\prime(x)f)(y)& = f(yx), \quad \forall x,y \in G.
    \eea
nodes.statement_short: Exact representation is the right regular action.

nodes.name: V is an isometry
nodes.statement:
$V$ is an isometry because $\rho(x)$ is unitary, yielding:
    \be
    V^* V(u) = \EE_{x \in G} \left[ \rho^*(x) \rho(x)(u) \right] = \EE_{x \in G} [u] = u.
    \ee

nodes.name: Averaging identity
nodes.statement:
The compression of the exact representation ``averages'' over group multiplication. For any $u \in \mathcal{H}$:
    \bea V^* \rho^\prime(x) V(u) & = & \EE_{y \in G} \left[ \rho^*(y) (\rho^\prime(x)\rho(y))(u) \right] \nonumber \\
    & = & \EE_{y \in G} \left[ \rho^*(y) \rho(yx)(u) \right].
    \eea

nodes.name: Compression averages over group multiplication
nodes.statement:
V^* \rho^\prime(x) V(u) & = & \EE_{y \in G} \left[ \rho^*(y) (\rho^\prime(x)\rho(y))(u) \right] \nonumber \\
    & = & \EE_{y \in G} \left[ \rho^*(y) \rho(yx)(u) \right].

nodes.name: Correlation equals pair-correlation
nodes.statement:
Substituting the average property from ~\equref{eq:isometry-average} into the inner product, and using the unitarity of $\rho(y)$ to rewrite the adjoints ($\langle A, B^* C \rangle_\sigma = \langle B A, C \rangle_\sigma$), we obtain:
    \bea \EE_{x \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\rangle_\sigma 
    & = & \EE_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), \rho^*(y) \rho(yx) \rangle_\sigma \nonumber \\ 
    & = & \EE_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle \rho(y)\rho(x), \rho(yx) \rangle_\sigma \nonumber \\ 
    & = & \mathcal{C}(\rho).
    \eea

nodes.name: Average correlation equals pair-correlation
nodes.statement:
\EE_{x \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\rangle_\sigma 
    & = & \EE_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), \rho^*(y) \rho(yx) \rangle_\sigma \nonumber \\ 
    & = & \EE_{x,y \in G} \Re \langle \rho(y)\rho(x), \rho(yx) \rangle_\sigma \nonumber \\ 
    & = & \mathcal{C}(\rho).

nodes.name: Apply definition
nodes.statement: By the definition of an $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-approximate representation, the pair-correlation inherently satisfies $\mathcal{C}(\rho) \geq 1 - \varepsilon$, which concludes the proof.

nodes.name: Gowers-Hatami theorem (regular-representation version)
nodes.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite group, \(\varepsilon \geq 0\), and \(\rho: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) on space $\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{C}^{d}$. Then there exists an isometry \(V: \mathcal{H} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) to a different space $\mathcal{H}^\prime$, and a representation \(\rho^\prime: G \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) such that \be \mathbb{E}_{x \in G}\left\|\rho(x)-V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \leq 2 \varepsilon. \ee
assumptions: \(\rho: G \rightarrow U(\mathcal{H})\) an \((\varepsilon, \sigma)\)-representation of \(G\) on space $\mathcal{H}=\mathbb{C}^{d}$
conclusions:
there exists an isometry \(V: \mathcal{H} \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) to a different space $\mathcal{H}^\prime$, 
and a representation \(\rho^\prime: G \rightarrow \mathcal{H}^\prime\) such that
nodes.statement_short: Approximate representations are $2\varepsilon$-close in average $\sigma$-norm to a compression of an exact representation.
nodes.label: gowers-hatami-2

nodes.name: Proof of Gowers-Hatami via regular representation
nodes.statement: A regular-representation proof of the Gowers-Hatami theorem appears in Morel's slides~\cite{Morel20}, following the original Gowers-Hatami theorem~\cite{GowHat17}. The rest of the proof follows by expanding the $\sigma$-norm, bounding the norm of $\EE_{x \in G} V^* \rho^\prime(x) V$ and applying the definition of $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-representation. In particular, we have \bea & &\EE_{x \in G}\left\|\rho(x)-V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \\ &= & \EE_{x \in G} \| \rho(x) \|_\sigma^2 + \EE_{x \in G} \|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma^2 - 2 \EE_{x \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\rangle_\sigma \nonumber \eea Because $\rho$ is unitary and $\Tr \sigma = 1$, $\EE_{x \in G} \| \rho(x) \|_\sigma^2 = 1$. For the second term, recall from \equref{eq:isometry-average} that the compression is the group average $V^* \rho^\prime(x) V = \EE_{y \in G} \rho^*(y)\rho(yx)$. Each summand $\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)$ is a product of unitaries, hence unitary, so $\|\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)\|_\sigma = 1$. By convexity of the $\sigma$-norm---the triangle inequality applied to the average---we obtain \be \|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma = \left\| \EE_{y \in G} \rho^*(y)\rho(yx) \right\|_\sigma \le \EE_{y \in G} \|\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)\|_\sigma = 1, \ee hence $\EE_{x \in G}\|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma^2 \le 1$. Therefore using the bounds in ~\equref{eq:isometry-unitary-bound} and ~\equref{eq:inner-product-bound} by applying Lemma~\ref{gowers-hatami-correlation}, we have \be \EE_{x \in G}\left\|\rho(x)-V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \le 2 - 2(1 - \varepsilon) = 2\varepsilon. \ee
nodes.statement_short: Expand the $\sigma$-norm into three terms; bound the compression norm by convexity and the cross term by the pair-correlation lemma.

nodes.name: Attribution
nodes.statement: A regular-representation proof of the Gowers-Hatami theorem appears in Morel's slides~\cite{Morel20}, following the original Gowers-Hatami theorem~\cite{GowHat17}.

nodes.name: Expand sigma-norm
nodes.statement:
The rest of the proof follows by expanding the $\sigma$-norm, bounding the norm of $\EE_{x \in G} V^* \rho^\prime(x) V$ and applying the definition of $(\varepsilon, \sigma)$-representation.
     In particular, we have 
     \bea
        & &\EE_{x \in G}\left\|\rho(x)-V^{*} \rho^\prime(x) V\right\|_{\sigma}^{2} \\ 
        &= & \EE_{x \in G} \| \rho(x) \|_\sigma^2 + \EE_{x \in G} \|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma^2 - 2 \EE_{x \in G} \Re \langle \rho(x), V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\rangle_\sigma \nonumber
    \eea
nodes.statement_short: Expand the squared $\sigma$-norm into three terms.

nodes.name: First term
nodes.statement: Because $\rho$ is unitary and $\Tr \sigma = 1$, $\EE_{x \in G} \| \rho(x) \|_\sigma^2 = 1$.

nodes.name: Second term
nodes.statement:
For the second term, recall from \equref{eq:isometry-average} that the compression is the group average $V^* \rho^\prime(x) V = \EE_{y \in G} \rho^*(y)\rho(yx)$. Each summand $\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)$ is a product of unitaries, hence unitary, so $\|\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)\|_\sigma = 1$. By convexity of the $\sigma$-norm---the triangle inequality applied to the average---we obtain
    \be \|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma = \left\| \EE_{y \in G} \rho^*(y)\rho(yx) \right\|_\sigma \le \EE_{y \in G} \|\rho^*(y)\rho(yx)\|_\sigma = 1,
    \ee
    hence $\EE_{x \in G}\|V^* \rho^\prime(x) V\|_\sigma^2 \le 1$.

nodes.name: Additivity and homogeneity
nodes.statement:
First notice that linearity implies two properties: 
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Additivity $f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y), \quad \forall x, y \in X$. 
    
    Note that for $q$ prime additivity is actually equivalent to linearity. However this is not the case for prime powers $q=p^s$ for $s > 1$.
    
    \item Homogeneity $f(a x) = a f(x), \quad \forall x \in X, \, a \in A$.

    For $q=2$, the two properties are redundant. 
    For $q > 2$, turns out testing homogeneity is crucial for a test to have a high soundness.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_short: Linearity implies additivity and homogeneity; additivity alone suffices only for prime $q$, and homogeneity testing matters for $q>2$.

nodes.name: Proof that G is an abelian group
nodes.statement: \emph{Associativity.} For $(x, a), (y, b), (z, c) \in G$, \begin{align*} \bigl((x, a) \star (y, b)\bigr) \star (z, c) &= (b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab) \star (z, c) = \bigl(b^{-1}c^{-1}x + a^{-1}c^{-1}y + a^{-1}b^{-1}z,\; abc\bigr), \end{align*} and an identical computation gives the same expression for $(x, a) \star \bigl((y, b) \star (z, c)\bigr)$. \emph{Commutativity.} $(y, b) \star (x, a) = (a^{-1}y + b^{-1}x,\; ba) = (b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab) = (x, a) \star (y, b).$ \emph{Identity.} For any $(y, b) \in G$, $(0, 1) \star (y, b) = (b^{-1}\cdot 0 + 1^{-1}\cdot y,\; 1\cdot b) = (y, b)$. \emph{Inverse.} For any $(x, a) \in G$, \[ (x, a) \star (-a^2 x, a^{-1}) = \bigl((a^{-1})^{-1}\cdot x + a^{-1}\cdot(-a^2 x),\; a\cdot a^{-1}\bigr) = (ax - ax,\; 1) = (0, 1). \]
nodes.statement_short: Verify associativity, commutativity, identity and inverses by direct computation.

nodes.name: Associativity
Commutativity

\emph{Commutativity.}
$(y, b) \star (x, a) = (a^{-1}y + b^{-1}x,\; ba) = (b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab) = (x, a) \star (y, b).$

nodes.name: Identity
nodes.statement:
\emph{Identity.} For any $(y, b) \in G$,
$(0, 1) \star (y, b) = (b^{-1}\cdot 0 + 1^{-1}\cdot y,\; 1\cdot b) = (y, b)$.

nodes.name: Inverse
nodes.statement:
\emph{Inverse.} For any $(x, a) \in G$,
\[
(x, a) \star (-a^2 x, a^{-1}) = \bigl((a^{-1})^{-1}\cdot x + a^{-1}\cdot(-a^2 x),\; a\cdot a^{-1}\bigr)
= (ax - ax,\; 1) = (0, 1).
\]

nodes.name: Group isomorphism to product group
nodes.statement: The map \be \Psi : G \to (X, +) \times (A, \cdot), \qquad \Psi(x, a) := (ax, a), \ee is a group isomorphism onto the direct product of $(X, +)$ and $(A, \cdot)$ with operation $\star_\Psi:(x,\; a) \star_\Psi (y,\; b) = (x+y,\; ab)$. Indeed, \[ \Psi\bigl((x, a) \star (y, b)\bigr) = \bigl(ab\cdot(b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y),\; ab\bigr) = (ax + by,\; ab) = \Psi(x, a) \star_\Psi \Psi(y, b), \] and $\Psi$ is bijective with inverse $\Psi^{-1}(y, b) = (b^{-1}y, b)$. This isomorphism is used only to \emph{motivate} the characters below. The Lean development does not formalize $\Psi$: it equips $G$ with its group structure (\lemref{lem:group}) and defines the characters $\chi_{\alpha,k}$ (\propref{prop:group_characaters}) directly on the twisted group, proving the homomorphism property by direct computation rather than by pulling back through $\Psi$. Accordingly it is recorded as a remark, with no \texttt{\textbackslash lean} link and no node in the dependency graph.
nodes.statement_short: $\Psi(x,a)=(ax,a)$ is an isomorphism from the twisted group to $(X,+)\times(A,\cdot)$; used only as motivation.

nodes.name: Pontryagin dual of a direct product

Like the isomorphism above, this is used only to motivate the character formula and is not part of the formalized graph.

conclusions: the Pontryagin dual (the set of irreducible characters) factors as $\hat{H} = \hat{G_1} \times \hat{G_2}$

nodes.name: Proof of group characters
nodes.statement: By the isomorphism $\Psi(x, a) = (ax, a)$ in the remark above, $(G, \star) \cong (X, +) \times (A, \cdot)$. First we consider the characters of the product group. Using the Pontryagin-dual factorization in the remark above, we have \[ \widehat{(X, +) \times (A, \cdot)} = \hat{X} \times \hat{A}. \] The character groups of $X$ and $A$ are \begin{align} \hat{X} &= \{\phi_\alpha(y) = \omega^{\Tr \inner{\alpha}{y}}\}_{\alpha\in X}, \\ \hat{A} &= \{\psi_k(b) =e^{\frac{i 2 \pi m k}{q-1}}\}_{k \in [0, \cdots, q-2]}, \end{align} where $b=g_0^m$ for a fixed multiplicative generator $g_0\in A$. Here the field trace $\Tr: \F_q \to \F_p$ is defined by $\Tr(x) = x + x^p + x^{p^2} + \cdots + x^{p^{s-1}}$ for $x \in \F_q$ (see Definition~1.1 in Chapter 1). Therefore, $\widehat{(X, +) \times (A, \cdot)} = \{\Theta_{\alpha, k}(y, b) = \phi_\alpha(y) \psi_k(b)\}_{\alpha, k}$. The character $\chi \in \hat{G}$ is given by the pull-back through the isomorphism \be \chi_{\alpha, k}(x, a) = \Theta_{\alpha, k}(\Psi(x, a)) = \Theta_{\alpha, k}(ax, a). \ee Therefore, we have $\chi_{\alpha, k}(x, a) = \phi_\alpha(ax) \psi_k(a) =\omega^{\Tr \inner{\alpha}{a x}} \psi_k(a)$.

First we observe that
\begin{equation} \Pr_{g, h \in G}\!\bigl[F_f(g \star h) = F_f(g)F_f(h)\bigr]
= \Pr_{c,d,x,y}\!\bigl[c f(x) + d f(y) = f(cx + dy)\bigr].

Using~\equref{eq:star} and~\equref{eq:Flift-def},

nodes.name: Alternative proof via Gowers-Hatami
nodes.statement: First denote \[ X := \F_q^n, \qquad A := \F_q^\times, \qquad \omega := e^{2\pi i/p}. \] Define a group $G$ on the set $X \times A$ with the binary operation \[ (x, a) \star (y, b) := \bigl(b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab\bigr). \] Let $F_f$ be the unitary matrix valued lift $F_f : G \to U(\cc^{q-1})$ given by the diagonal matrix \[ F_f(x, a) = D(a f(x)) := \sum_{c \in A} \omega^{\Tr\, c a f(x)}\ket{c}\bra{c}, \] where $\{\ket{c}\}$ denotes the orthonormal basis vectors of a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H} \cong \cc^{q-1}$, the inner product between operators is $\inner{A}{B}_\sigma=\Tr(A^* B \sigma)$, and $\sigma = \I/(q-1)$. By \lemref{lem:rep-iff-blr}, since $f$ is rejected with probability $\varepsilon$, the lift $F_f$ is a $(\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon,\frac{\I}{q-1})$ approximate representation of $(G, \star)$. Then by \lemref{lem:gh_linearity_formalized}, there exists a linear function $\ell: \FF_q^n \to \FF_q$ whose relative Hamming distance to $f$ is bounded by \[ \delta(f, \ell) \le \frac{q-1}{q}\cdot\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon = \varepsilon. \] This proves the claim \[ \delta(f, \lin) := \min_{\alpha} \delta(f, \ell_\alpha) \leq \delta(f, \ell) \leq \varepsilon. \] Miraculously, the loose factor $\frac{q}{q-1}$ in the approximate-representation parameter cancels the tighter factor $\frac{q-1}{q}$ of \lemref{lem:gh_linearity_formalized}. In Lean this route is formalized as \texttt{gh\_blr\_soundness\_acceptance}, which proves \texttt{acceptanceProbabilityBLR f $\le$ 1 - distanceToLinear f} (the statement of \texttt{blr\_soundness}), valid for $\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon\le1$; the unconditional statement is the direct proof above, since for $\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon>1$ the third-moment extraction's $\max\ge0$ step fails.
nodes.statement_short: Lift $f$ to an approximate representation of the twisted group and apply the Gowers-Hatami linearity lemma; the factors $q/(q-1)$ cancel.

nodes.name: Recall setup
nodes.statement:
First denote
\[
X := \F_q^n, \qquad A := \F_q^\times, \qquad \omega := e^{2\pi i/p}.
\]
Define a group $G$ on the set $X \times A$ with the binary operation
\[
(x, a) \star (y, b) := \bigl(b^{-1}x + a^{-1}y,\; ab\bigr).
\]
Let $F_f$ be the unitary matrix valued lift $F_f : G \to U(\cc^{q-1})$ given by the diagonal matrix
\[
F_f(x, a) = D(a f(x)) := \sum_{c \in A} \omega^{\Tr\, c a f(x)}\ket{c}\bra{c},
\]
where $\{\ket{c}\}$ denotes the orthonormal basis vectors of a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H} \cong \cc^{q-1}$, the
inner product between operators is $\inner{A}{B}_\sigma=\Tr(A^* B \sigma)$, and $\sigma = \I/(q-1)$.

nodes.name: Lift is approximate representation
nodes.statement:
By
\lemref{lem:rep-iff-blr}, since $f$ is rejected with probability $\varepsilon$, the lift $F_f$ is a
$(\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon,\frac{\I}{q-1})$ approximate representation of $(G, \star)$.

nodes.name: Apply GH linearity
nodes.statement:
Then by \lemref{lem:gh_linearity_formalized}, there exists a linear function $\ell: \FF_q^n \to \FF_q$ whose
relative Hamming distance to $f$ is bounded by
\[
    \delta(f, \ell) \le \frac{q-1}{q}\cdot\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon = \varepsilon.
\]
This proves the claim
\[
\delta(f, \lin) := \min_{\alpha} \delta(f, \ell_\alpha) \leq \delta(f, \ell) \leq \varepsilon.
\]

nodes.name: Factor cancellation
nodes.statement:
Miraculously, the loose factor $\frac{q}{q-1}$ in the approximate-representation parameter cancels the tighter
factor $\frac{q-1}{q}$ of \lemref{lem:gh_linearity_formalized}.

nodes.name: Lean scope note
nodes.statement:
In Lean this route is formalized as \texttt{gh\_blr\_soundness\_acceptance}, which proves
\texttt{acceptanceProbabilityBLR f $\le$ 1 - distanceToLinear f} (the statement of \texttt{blr\_soundness}),
valid for $\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon\le1$; the unconditional statement is the direct proof above, since for
$\frac{q}{q-1}\varepsilon>1$ the third-moment extraction's $\max\ge0$ step fails.

nodes.statement: An \emph{oracle context} is a bundle consisting of an oracle specification and a query implementation for that specification.
nodes.label: OracleContext

nodes.name: Randomness oracle
nodes.statement: As \emph{randomness oracle}, we will use the {uniform sampling query implementation} for the randomness oracle specification.
nodes.label: randOracle

nodes.name: Oracle computation
nodes.statement: An \emph{oracle computation} is a monadic computation in the free monad generated by an oracle specification, i.e. a description (a ``script'') of a program consisting of a chain of oracle queries (compatible with any query implementation of the specification) and deterministic Lean computations.
nodes.genus: monadic computation in the free monad generated by an oracle specification
nodes.label: OracleComp

nodes.name: Verifier
nodes.statement:
A \emph{verifier} is a function that takes an input \(x \in \{0,1\}^*\) and produces an oracle computation
(with query access to a randomness oracle) that outputs a boolean. This definition can be extended to include
other oracles (typically a proof oracle).

nodes.name: Unit verifier
nodes.statement: A \emph{unit verifier} (or just \emph{verifier} when it is clear from the context) is an oracle computation with query access to a randomness oracle that outputs a boolean.

nodes.name: Time complexity
nodes.statement: The price to pay for using these definitions for verifiers instead of Turing machines is that we have no simple way to enforce the time complexity of the verifier. For that, a possible approach would be to restrict the allowed operations to a strict set of operations instead of general Lean computations, and track the time cost using query complexity.

nodes.name: PCP verifier
nodes.statement: A \emph{PCP verifier} is a verifier with query access to a function $\pi : [\ell (|x|)] \to \Sigma$.
differentia: with query access to a function $\pi : [\ell (|x|)] \to \Sigma$
nodes.label: PCPVerifier

nodes.name: PCP complexity class
nodes.statement: A language $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ is in $\PCP[\varepsilon_c, \varepsilon_s, \Sigma, \ell, q, r]$ if there exists a polynomial-time PCP verifier $V$ such that for every $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $V$ makes at most $q(|x|)$ queries to the proof oracle and at most $r(|x|)$ randomness queries, and the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item Completeness: If $x \in L$, then $\exists \pi \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)}, \, \Pr\left[V^\pi(x)=1 \right] \geq 1 - \varepsilon_c$. \item Soundness: If $x \notin L$, then $\forall \widetilde{\pi} \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)},\, \Pr\left[V^{\widetilde{\pi}}(x)=1 \right] \leq \varepsilon_s$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Languages with a poly-time PCP verifier of given completeness/soundness error, alphabet, proof length, query and randomness bounds.
nodes.label: PCP

nodes.name: LPCP verifier
nodes.statement: A \emph{LPCP verifier} is a verifier with query access to a linear function $\langle \pi,\cdot \rangle : \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)} \to \Sigma$.
nodes.label: LPCPVerifier

nodes.name: LPCP complexity class
nodes.statement: A language $L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$ is in $\LPCP[\varepsilon_c, \varepsilon_s, \Sigma, \ell, q, r]$ if there exists a polynomial-time LPCP verifier $V$ such that for every $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, $V$ makes at most $q(|x|)$ queries to the linear proof oracle and at most $r(|x|)$ randomness queries, and the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item Completeness: If $x \in L$, then $\exists \pi \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)}, \, \Pr\left[V^{\langle \pi, \cdot \rangle}(x)=1 \right] \geq 1 - \varepsilon_c$. \item Soundness: If $x \notin L$, then $\forall \widetilde{\pi} \in \Sigma^{\ell(|x|)},\, \Pr\left[V^{\langle \widetilde{\pi}, \cdot \rangle}(x)=1 \right] \leq \varepsilon_s$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Same as PCP but the verifier queries a linear function $\langle\pi,\cdot\rangle$.
nodes.label: LPCP

nodes.name: BLR verifier over F_2
nodes.statement: Let \(V_{\mathrm{BLR}(\F_{2}, n)}^{f}\) be the verifier with oracle access to \(f: \F_{2}^n \to \F_{2}\) defined as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Sample \(x, y \leftarrow \F_2^n\). \item Accept if and only if \(f(x) + f(y) = f(x+y)\). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: BLR.basicVerifier

nodes.name: Sample x, y
nodes.statement: Sample \(x, y \leftarrow \F_2^n\).

nodes.name: Accept test
nodes.statement: Accept if and only if \(f(x) + f(y) = f(x+y)\).

nodes.name: BLR completeness over F_2
nodes.statement: Let \(n > 0\). For every linear function \(f: \F_{2}^n \to \F_{2}\), we have \[\Pr \left[V_{\mathrm{BLR}(\F_{2}, n)}^{f} = 1\right] = 1.\]
nodes.label: BLR_basic_completeness_ZMod2

nodes.name: BLR soundness over F_2
nodes.statement: Let \(n > 0\) and \(f: \F_{2}^n \to \F_{2}\). \[\Pr \left[V_{\mathrm{BLR}(\F_{2}, n)}^{f} = 1\right] \leq 1 - \distanceToLin{f}.\]
nodes.label: BLR_basic_soundness_ZMod2

nodes.name: LINEQ
nodes.statement: For a field \(\F\) and parameters \(m, n \in \N\), we define the language \[\LINEQ(\F,m,n) := \{ (M, c) \in \F^{m\times n} \times \F^{m} \mid \exists b\in \F^n, \, Mb = c \}.\]
nodes.label: LINEQ

nodes.name: LPCP verifier for LINEQ
nodes.statement: Let \(V_{\LINEQ(\F,m,n)}^{\langle b, \cdot \rangle } (M,c)\) be the LPCP verifier defined as follows: \begin{enumerate} \item Sample \(r \leftarrow \F^m\). \item Query \(b\in \F^n \) at \(u:= \Transpose{M}r \in \F^n\). \item Accept if and only if \(\langle b,u\rangle = \langle c, r\rangle\). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Sample $r$, query the linear proof at $M^\top r$, accept iff it equals $\langle c,r\rangle$.
nodes.label: LINEQ.verifier

nodes.name: Sample r
nodes.statement: Sample \(r \leftarrow \F^m\).

nodes.name: Query proof
nodes.statement: Query \(b\in \F^n \) at \(u:= \Transpose{M}r \in \F^n\).

nodes.name: Accept test
nodes.statement: Accept if and only if \(\langle b,u\rangle = \langle c, r\rangle\).

nodes.name: Nonzero linear form vanishing probability
nodes.statement: Let \(a\in\F^m\) be nonzero. Then \[ |\F|\cdot\Pr_{r\leftarrow\F^m}\!\left[\langle a,r\rangle=0\right]\leq 1. \] Equivalently, a nonzero linear form over \(\F^m\) vanishes on a uniformly random input with probability at most \(1/|\F|\).
nodes.label: LINEQ.linear_form_uniform_prob_mul_card_le_one

nodes.name: Proof of linear form vanishing probability
nodes.statement: Choose a coordinate \(i\) with \(a_i\neq 0\). After fixing all other coordinates of \(r\), there is exactly one value of \(r_i\) making \(\langle a,r\rangle=0\).
nodes.statement_short: Fix all but a coordinate with $a_i\ne0$; exactly one value of $r_i$ works.

nodes.name: Linear PCP for LINEQ
nodes.statement: \[\LINEQ(\F,m,n) \in \LPCP\left[\varepsilon_c=0, \varepsilon_s= 1 / |\F|, \Sigma = \F, \ell = |x|, q = 1, r = m\right].\]
nodes.statement_short: LINEQ has a one-query LPCP with perfect completeness and soundness $1/|\F|$.

nodes.name: Proof of LINEQ LPCP
nodes.statement: Consider the LPCP verifier \(V_{\LINEQ(\F,m,n)}^{\langle b, \cdot \rangle } (M,c)\).\\ \emph{Completeness:} If \(Mb =c\), then for every \(r \in \F^m\), we have \[\langle b, u \rangle = \Transpose{b} (\Transpose{M} r) = \Transpose{(Mb)} r = \langle c , r\rangle.\] \emph{Soundness:} If \(Mb \neq c\), then \begin{gather*} \Pr_{r\leftarrow \F^m} \left[\langle b, u \rangle = \langle c , r\rangle \right] = \Pr_{r\leftarrow \F^m} \left[\langle Mb, r \rangle = \langle c , r\rangle \right] \\= \Pr_{r\leftarrow \F^m} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{m} (Mb - c)_{i} \cdot r_{i} = 0\right] \leq 1 / |\F|, \end{gather*} where the last inequality follows from \ref{LINEQ.linear_form_uniform_prob_mul_card_le_one}.
nodes.statement_short: Completeness by transposition; soundness by the nonzero linear form lemma.

Tensor product of vectors
nodes.statement:
For a field \(\F\), vectors \(a \in \F^n\) and \(b \in \F^m\), the tensor product \(a \otimes b \in \F^{n \times m}\)
is the matrix defined by
\[
  (a \otimes b)_{i,j} := a_i b_j \quad \forall i \in [n],\, j \in [m].
\]

nodes.name: Flattening
nodes.statement: We write \(\mathrm{flat}(a \otimes b) \in \F^{nm}\) for the row-concatenation of \(a \otimes b\).

nodes.name: TENSORQ
nodes.statement: For a field \(\F\) and \(n \in \N\), define the tensor test language \[ \mathrm{TENSORQ}(\F, n) := \bigl\{ (a, b) \in \F^n \times \F^{n^2} \mid b = \mathrm{flat}(a \otimes a) \bigr\}. \]
nodes.label: TENSORQ

nodes.name: LPCP verifier for TENSORQ
nodes.statement: Given \((a,b) \in \F^n \times \F^{n^2}\), the LPCP verifier \(V_{\mathrm{TENSORQ}(\F,n)}^{\langle \pi,\cdot\rangle}(a,b)\) uses a proof \(\pi=\alpha\parallel\beta \in \F^{n+n^2}\), intended to be the linear encoding of the public input \((a,b)\). Since the proof may be dishonest, the verifier checks consistency with \((a,b)\) on the sampled queries before checking the tensor relation: \begin{enumerate} \item Sample \(s,t \leftarrow \F^n\). \item Query the \(\alpha\)-part of \(\pi\) at \(s\) and at \(t\), obtaining \(y_s\) and \(y_t\). \item Query the \(\beta\)-part of \(\pi\) at \(\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\), obtaining \(y_{s,t}\). \item Accept if and only if \[ y_s=\langle a,s\rangle,\qquad y_t=\langle a,t\rangle,\qquad y_{s,t}=\langle b,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle,\qquad y_{s,t}=y_s y_t. \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Sample $s,t$, query the proof at $s$, $t$ and $\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)$, check consistency with $(a,b)$ and $y_{s,t}=y_sy_t$.
nodes.label: TENSORQ.verifier

nodes.name: Sample s, t
nodes.statement: Sample \(s,t \leftarrow \F^n\).

nodes.name: Query alpha-part
nodes.statement: Query the \(\alpha\)-part of \(\pi\) at \(s\) and at \(t\), obtaining \(y_s\) and \(y_t\).

nodes.name: Query beta-part
nodes.statement: Query the \(\beta\)-part of \(\pi\) at \(\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\), obtaining \(y_{s,t}\).

nodes.statement:
Accept if and only if
  \[
      y_s=\langle a,s\rangle,\qquad
      y_t=\langle a,t\rangle,\qquad
      y_{s,t}=\langle b,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle,\qquad
      y_{s,t}=y_s y_t.
    \]

nodes.name: Tensor self-check
nodes.statement: In settings where \(a\) and \(b\) are supplied only by the proof oracle, the tensor self-check uses the same three queries but has no public input to compare against. Given oracle access to \(\pi=\alpha\parallel\beta\in\F^{n+n^2}\), sample \(s,t\leftarrow\F^n\), query \[ y_s=\langle\alpha,s\rangle,\qquad y_t=\langle\alpha,t\rangle,\qquad y_{s,t}=\langle\beta,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle, \] and accept if and only if \(y_{s,t}=y_s y_t\). This is the tensor component used inside the QESAT verifier.
nodes.statement_short: Query $\alpha$ at $s,t$ and $\beta$ at $\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)$ and accept iff $y_{s,t}=y_sy_t$.

nodes.statement: For every \(a,s,t\in\F^n\), \[ \langle \mathrm{flat}(a\otimes a),\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle = \langle a,s\rangle \langle a,t\rangle. \]

nodes.name: Proof of tensor check completeness
nodes.statement: \begin{align*} \langle \mathrm{flat}(a\otimes a),\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle &= \sum_{i,j} a_i a_j s_i t_j = \left(\sum_i a_i s_i\right)\left(\sum_j a_j t_j\right) = \langle a,s\rangle \langle a,t\rangle. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Bilinear reduction
nodes.statement:
For each \(i \in [n]\) define the linear polynomial \(p_i(t) := \sum_{j \in [n]} (b_{ij} - a_i a_j)\, t_j\).
For fixed \(s,t\), if the verifier accepts, then its consistency checks force

\(y_{s,t}=\langle b,\mathrm{flat}(s\otimes t)\rangle\). Thus acceptance can only occur when

\]
